headline: Burnham opens door to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement ahead of 20 November summit

terms.meaning: The right of people in EU countries to live and work in any other member country.
The EU trading zone with shared rules and no trade barriers between members.
The EU area where people cross borders without passport checks.

levels.headline: Burnham opens door to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement ahead of 20 November summit
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told the Sunday Times he is open to an "honest discussion" about the UK readopting EU free movement as part of its future relationship with Brussels, while ruling out joining the euro or the Schengen passport-free zone.
The comments come ahead of a UK-EU summit on 20 November, where Mr Burnham and EU leaders hope to strike deals on food and drink, youth mobility and emissions trading. The question of reciprocal youth mobility has pushed free movement up the agenda.
Mr Burnham has committed to Sir Keir Starmer's 2024 manifesto, which ruled out free movement, single market membership and a customs union. He has suggested any major change might need a mandate at the next general election, which is not expected before 2029, and has said a referendum "wouldn't be the right thing to do right now".
Reform UK's Nigel Farage called the remarks a "total betrayal of Brexit Britain", while Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "unpicking" the Brexit withdrawal agreement.
levels.why: It shapes how the UK trades, who can work here and what the next election is fought on.

levels.headline: Burnham says he is open to talking about EU free movement before next month's summit
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is open to an "honest discussion" about bringing back EU free movement as part of closer ties with the European Union. He told the Sunday Times the UK would not join the euro or the Schengen zone, which lets people cross borders without passport checks.
A UK-EU summit is due on 20 November. Both sides hope to agree deals on food and drink, youth mobility and emissions trading. Youth mobility means letting young people live and work in each other's countries for a period, and it has pushed free movement to the top of the agenda.
Mr Burnham has promised to stick to Sir Keir Starmer's 2024 manifesto, which ruled out free movement, the single market and a customs union. Any big change might be put to voters at the next general election, which is not expected before 2029. He has said a referendum is not right now.
Nigel Farage called his remarks a "total betrayal of Brexit Britain". Kemi Badenoch said he was "unpicking" the Brexit deal.
levels.why: Relations with the EU affect trade, jobs and travel, and the debate is likely to dominate the coming months.

levels.headline: Burnham open to debate on free movement as UK-EU summit nears
levels.body:
Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, has said he wants an "honest discussion" about the UK returning to EU free movement, the right of people to live and work across EU countries. He made clear the UK would not join the euro or the Schengen area, where border checks are removed.
He and EU leaders meet at a summit on 20 November. They hope to reach agreements on food and drink, on youth mobility schemes, and on emissions trading, a system that puts a price on pollution. The youth mobility question has made free movement a bigger topic than expected.
The Labour manifesto of 2024, which Mr Burnham says he is bound by, ruled out free movement, single market membership and a customs union. He has hinted that bigger changes would need voters' approval at the next general election, not expected before 2029, and does not think a referendum is right now.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage called it a betrayal of Brexit. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the Prime Minister was unpicking the withdrawal agreement.
levels.why: Whatever is agreed with the EU could change trade, travel and work for people across the UK.

levels.headline: Prime Minister says he will have an 'honest discussion' about EU free movement
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is ready to have an "honest discussion" about bringing back free movement with the European Union. Free movement lets people live and work in any EU country. He told the Sunday Times the UK would still not join the euro or the Schengen zone.
The talk comes before a summit with EU leaders on 20 November. The two sides hope to agree new deals on food and drink, on letting young people live and work abroad, and on a scheme that puts a price on carbon emissions.
The Labour manifesto from 2024 said no to free movement, the single market and a customs union, and Mr Burnham says he will keep to it. He suggested larger changes could be put to voters at the next election, which is not expected before 2029. He does not think a referendum is the right step now.
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, called his comments a betrayal of Brexit, and Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said he was undoing the Brexit deal.
levels.why: The UK's future relationship with the EU matters for trade, jobs and young people's chances to study and work abroad.

levels.headline: Burnham ready to talk about free movement with the EU
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is open to a frank talk about bringing back free movement with the European Union. That is the right of people to live and work in each other's countries. He has ruled out joining the euro, the shared EU currency, and the Schengen zone, where people cross borders without passport checks.
The UK and the EU hold a summit on 20 November. Both hope to agree deals on food and drink, on young people living and working abroad for a time, and on the trading of carbon emissions. The idea of young people moving more freely has made the wider free movement question much more important.
Mr Burnham says he will stick to Labour's 2024 promises, which ruled out free movement, the single market and a customs union. If he wants more change, he may ask voters at the next election, not expected before 2029. He says a referendum is not right now.
Critics are angry. Nigel Farage called it a betrayal of Brexit, and Kemi Badenoch said it undoes the Brexit deal.
levels.why: Decisions on EU ties can change prices, travel rules and job and study options for people in Britain.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister says he is willing to talk about free movement with the EU
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is willing to talk openly about free movement with the European Union. Free movement means people can live and work in other EU countries without needing a visa. He has said Britain will not join the euro, which is the money many EU countries use, or the Schengen zone, where people cross borders without passport checks.
On 20 November, the UK and EU leaders will meet. They hope to agree deals on food and drink, on letting young people spend time living and working in each other's countries, and on a scheme to put a price on pollution.
In 2024, Labour promised not to bring back free movement. Mr Burnham says he will keep that promise for now. If he wants bigger changes, he may ask voters at the next general election, which is not expected before 2029. He does not think a vote on rejoining is right now.
Some politicians are angry. Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch both criticised him.
levels.why: Britain's links with Europe affect what we buy, where we can travel and where young people can work.

levels.headline: Prime Minister Burnham wants to talk about people moving freely between the UK and the EU
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says he wants to have an honest talk about people moving more freely between the UK and the European Union. This was called free movement before Brexit. It meant a person from the UK could live and work in France, and a person from France could live and work here.
He says Britain will not use the euro or join the Schengen area, where people cross borders without showing a passport. Next month, on 20 November, he will meet EU leaders. They want to agree deals on food, on young people living abroad for a while, and on cutting pollution.
Before the last election, Labour promised not to bring back free movement. Mr Burnham says he will keep that promise. If he wanted to change it, he might ask voters at the next election, which is not expected before 2029.
Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch are not happy. They say it goes against Brexit.
levels.why: It could change how easily people can live and work in Europe, and how the UK trades with its neighbours.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister wants to talk about people moving between the UK and Europe
levels.body:
Andy Burnham is the Prime Minister. He leads the government. He says he wants to talk about letting people move more easily between the UK and countries in the European Union, or EU. The EU is a group of European countries that work together.
Before Brexit, a person from Britain could go and live and work in an EU country. People from those countries could do the same here. Brexit ended that. Mr Burnham says he is open to talking about it again. He says the UK will not use the euro, the money many EU countries share.
On 20 November, he will meet EU leaders. They hope to agree new deals on food and drink and on young people spending time working abroad.
Mr Burnham has said he will keep Labour's promise from the last election, which was not to bring back free movement. Some other politicians are cross. They think Brexit should stay as it is.
levels.why: The choice affects trade, jobs and whether young people can live and work in Europe.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister is willing to talk about moving to and from Europe
levels.body:
The Prime Minister is the person who runs the government. His name is Andy Burnham. He says he is ready to talk about letting people from the UK and from Europe live and work in each other's countries more easily.
A few years ago, Britain left the European Union, or EU. The EU is a group of countries in Europe that work together. After Britain left, it became harder to live and work in those countries. Mr Burnham says he will talk about this again, but he says Britain will not use the euro. The euro is the money that many EU countries share.
He will meet EU leaders on 20 November. They want to agree on things like food, drink and young people working abroad.
Some politicians are very unhappy. They think Britain should stay out. Mr Burnham says he will not make any big change without asking voters first.
levels.why: It could change where people can live, work and study, and how Britain gets along with its neighbours.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister talks about Britain and its neighbours
levels.body:
Imagine your school is in a big group of schools. The schools used to share things. Pupils could visit other schools and join in lessons. Then your school left the group, and visiting got harder. That is a bit like Britain and the European Union, which is a group of countries in Europe.
The Prime Minister is the grown-up who leads the country. He is called Andy Burnham. He says he is ready to talk about making it easier again for people to go and live and work in those countries. He says Britain will not share their money, called the euro.
He will meet the leaders of the group next month. They want to agree on small things first, like food and drink, and young people working abroad for a while.
Some people like the idea. Some people are cross. Mr Burnham says that big changes would need voters to have their say.
levels.why: It matters because it could change how easily families, students and workers can travel and work in Europe.

headline: Wall Street ends lower on Friday as oil above $100 hits the Dow; S&P 500 down 0.52% at 7,623.68

levels.headline: Wall Street ends lower on Friday as oil above $100 hits the Dow; S&P 500 down 0.52% at 7,623.68
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down 0.52% at 7,623.68 on Friday 23 October, the last completed US trading session, with all three main indexes lower. Monday's session was still to begin when this edition was written.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to settle at 52,215.16. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 0.21% to 25,955.34, according to CNBC, though another source showed it as roughly flat.
CNBC reported that a sell-off in technology shares on the previous day spread to other parts of the market, while US oil prices topped $100 a barrel amid tensions in the Middle East. Higher energy costs have fed worries about inflation and interest rates.
For the week, the S&P 500 lost 0.5% and the Nasdaq shed 0.7%, while the Dow gained 0.4%. Investors now look ahead to a busy week of central bank decisions, including the US Federal Reserve on Wednesday 28 October.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions, savings and company investment, and they signal how worried investors are about inflation.

CNBC said a sell-off in tech shares on Thursday spread to other sectors, and US oil rose above $100 a barrel because of tensions in the Middle East. Dearer energy makes people worry that prices will keep rising and that interest rates will go up.
Over the whole week, the S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the Nasdaq fell 0.7%, but the Dow rose 0.4%. This week the US central bank, the Federal Reserve, makes its next rates decision.
levels.why: What happens to shares can affect pension pots and show whether investors are nervous.

levels.headline: Pocket money and the share market
levels.body:
Imagine a school fair where children swap cards. Each card is a little bit like a share. A share is a tiny piece of a company. Cards can be worth more or less each day, depending on how many children want them.
On Friday, the cards in America were worth a little less. There are three big lists that grown-ups use to check. One list has 500 big companies, one has 30, and one has lots of tech companies. All three went down a little. The biggest fall was in the list of 30.
One reason is that oil cost more than $100 for each barrel. Oil makes petrol for cars. When it costs more, lots of things in the shops can cost more too. That makes grown-ups worried.
On Wednesday, the people in charge of America's main bank will decide what to do about interest rates. That is like deciding the price of borrowing pocket money.
levels.why: It matters because the cost of petrol and food affects every family, and share prices show how worried investors feel.

headline: Healey's first Budget arrives on Wednesday with gilt yields near 19-year highs

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget arrives on Wednesday with gilt yields near 19-year highs
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will deliver his first Budget on Wednesday 28 October. The government says it will move "power and money out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain".
The backdrop is tough. The 10-year gilt yield was around 5.37% in the latest quote found, after reaching a 19-year high earlier this autumn. Euronews reported it just below 5.4% at the end of September. Markets are also pricing in further Bank of England rate rises, with reports of at least three 25 basis point increases by April 2027, as UK inflation reached 3.5% in September.
UK public sector net debt is above £3 trillion. One analysis says investors seem to be giving Mr Healey the benefit of the doubt, with gilt markets unusually calm despite concerns over ambitious spending plans that have yet to be fully costed.
No measures have been announced yet, so details of any tax or spending changes remain to be seen on Wednesday.
levels.why: The Budget sets taxes and spending, and the reaction of bond markets limits how much the government can borrow.

levels.headline: Britain's money plan is announced on Wednesday

levels.why: It decides how much tax people pay and how much the government can spend on schools and hospitals.

headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% in September as motor fuel costs surge

terms.meaning: Consumer Prices Index, the main measure of how fast prices are rising.

levels.headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% in September as motor fuel costs surge
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in the 12 months to September from 3.1% in August, the Office for National Statistics said on 21 October. Economists had forecast 3.4%.
Motor fuel was the main driver, with prices up 29.8% on a year earlier, and transport made the largest contribution to the rise. Prices rose 0.4% on the month. CPIH, which includes owner occupiers' housing costs, rose to 3.6% from 3.3%. Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, rose to 2.8%, its highest since September 2023. Food inflation held at 1.3%.
Producer prices also climbed. Input prices rose 8.3% year on year and factory-gate output prices rose 4.6%, the largest rise since April 2023.
The figures strengthen expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates in November. The ONS will publish October's figures on 18 November.

levels.headline: Markets price near-certain Bank of England rate rise to 4% in November after inflation surprise
levels.body:
Markets see a 98% chance that the Bank of England will raise Bank Rate by 25 basis points to 4% at its November meeting, according to LSEG data cited by CNBC after UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September. Most traders also expect another 25 point rise in December.
In September the Monetary Policy Committee held Bank Rate at 3.75%, but the vote was 6 to 3. The three dissenters wanted an increase to 4%. Governor Andrew Bailey said the more likely it was that volatility persisted, the more likely it was that Bank Rate would need to rise to bring inflation back to the 2% target.
One economist said services inflation had accelerated in recent months, raising concern about second-round effects, meaning energy costs spreading into wages and wider prices. Another tied the energy shock to the Middle East conflict.
A rate rise would make mortgages and loans more expensive for many households.
levels.why: Interest rate decisions set the cost of mortgages and loans for millions of households.

headline: US inflation climbs to 3.7% in September as petrol prices surge

terms.meaning: Consumer price inflation leaving out food and energy.

levels.headline: US inflation climbs to 3.7% in September as petrol prices surge
levels.body:
US consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, up from 3.4% in August and above the 3.6% economists expected, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on 14 October. Prices rose 0.6% on the month, in line with forecasts.
Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 2.6% on the year against an estimate of 2.5%, and 0.3% on the month, ahead of the 0.2% forecast. Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% and accounted for about half of the headline increase. Airline fares were up 22% over the past year, largely reflecting higher jet fuel costs.
Economists also pointed to tariffs, the build-out of artificial intelligence data centres and strong consumer demand. One economist said the core reading showed inflation was broad-based, not just fuel.
Markets expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates again this year, and the next CPI report is due on 10 November.
levels.why: US inflation influences Federal Reserve decisions, which ripple through global borrowing costs and markets.

levels.body:

Petrol is the biggest reason. It cost more because oil costs more. Plane tickets cost more too. There are also taxes on things that come from other countries. They are called tariffs.

levels.why: It matters because America is a very big country, and what happens there can affect prices everywhere.

headline: Fed, ECB and Bank of Japan expected to hold rates in a pivotal week, with a December US hike priced in

terms.meaning: The US central bank, which sets US interest rates.

levels.headline: Fed, ECB and Bank of Japan expected to hold rates in a pivotal week, with a December US hike priced in
levels.body:
Traders expect the Federal Reserve to leave interest rates unchanged when its two-day meeting ends on Wednesday 28 October, CNBC reported. CME FedWatch data from Friday showed about 92% odds of a hold, and about a 78% probability of a hike in December. The Fed's target range is currently 3.75% to 4%.
Bank of America is a notable dissenter, expecting a quarter-point rise this week, which it described as a "heavy lift". Stronger-than-expected US consumer and producer inflation data last week strengthened the case for tighter policy later this year.
The European Central Bank is due to announce its decision on Thursday 29 October, and it and the Bank of Japan are also expected to hold. US PCE inflation data is due on 29 October.
Oil-driven inflation is the main driver of rate-hike bets. Euro-area inflation has climbed to 3.8%. The probabilities are a snapshot and may shift.
levels.why: These decisions set borrowing costs across the world's largest economies and move currencies, shares and bonds.

Higher oil prices are the main reason traders think rates will rise. Euro-area inflation has risen to 3.8%.
levels.why: These decisions affect the cost of borrowing and the value of savings and shares.

levels.headline: Big central banks make rate decisions this week
levels.body:
A central bank is a bank for a whole country or region. It sets the interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. This week, the US central bank, the Federal Reserve, makes its decision on Wednesday 28 October. Traders expect no change. A tool called CME FedWatch showed a 92% chance of that. It also showed a 78% chance that rates will rise in December. The Fed's rate is now between 3.75% and 4%.
Bank of America thinks the Fed will raise rates this week by a quarter of a point. It admits that would be hard to do. Inflation figures last week were higher than expected. That makes higher rates more likely later this year.
The European Central Bank decides on Thursday 29 October. It and the Bank of Japan are also expected to keep rates the same.
levels.why: Rates decide how much it costs to borrow, and they affect shares, savings and currencies.

levels.headline: Central banks decide on interest rates this week
levels.body:
A central bank is the main bank of a country or a group of countries. It sets the interest rate. That is the extra money people pay when they borrow. This week, the US central bank, the Federal Reserve, decides on Wednesday 28 October. Traders think it will not change the rate. A tool called CME FedWatch says there is a 92% chance of that. It also says there is a 78% chance the rate will go up in December. The rate is now between 3.75% and 4%.
One big bank, Bank of America, thinks the rate will go up this week. It says that would be hard to do.
Prices in the US rose faster than experts expected last week. That makes higher rates more likely later this year.
The European Central Bank decides on Thursday. It is also expected to keep rates the same.
levels.why: It matters because interest rates decide how much borrowing costs and how much savers earn.

levels.headline: Big banks decide about interest this week
levels.body:
Some countries have a main bank, called a central bank. It decides how much extra people must pay when they borrow money. That extra money is called interest. The main bank in the United States is called the Federal Reserve. It will decide on Wednesday.
People who watch money think the bank will keep interest the same. Most of them are sure about it. They think that it might go up in December, because prices are rising faster.
One big bank, called Bank of America, thinks interest might go up this week. But most people do not.
On Thursday, the main bank for countries that use the euro will decide too. This is called the European Central Bank. People think it will keep interest the same.
Why does it matter? Interest changes how much loans cost.
levels.why: It matters because loans, mortgages and savings can all change when interest changes.

levels.headline: Big banks decide about the price of borrowing
levels.body:
Some countries have a main bank. It is called a central bank. It decides how much extra people must pay when they borrow. This extra money is called interest.
This week, the main bank of the United States will decide. It will do that on Wednesday. Many people think it will keep the price the same. But many also think it might go up in December. That is because prices in shops are rising faster.
On Thursday, another main bank will decide. It is for countries that use the euro, which is a kind of money. People think it will keep the price the same too.
Why does this matter? When borrowing costs more, loans and mortgages cost more. When it costs less, they cost less. It can also change how much money savers get.
levels.why: It matters because borrowing costs affect families, shops and businesses.

levels.headline: The bosses of money decide this week
levels.body:
Imagine a big bank for the whole country. It is called a central bank. It decides how much extra money you pay if you borrow some. That extra money is called interest.
This week, the main bank in America is going to decide. People think it will keep the price the same. Another big bank in Europe will decide too. People think it will keep the price the same as well.
Why would they change it? If prices in shops go up too fast, a bank can make borrowing cost more. Then people borrow and spend less, and prices slow down.
Prices have been going up because oil costs more. So some people think the banks might make borrowing cost more later this year.
levels.why: It matters because when borrowing costs more, families can feel it in their loans.

levels.headline: Why the money bosses matter
levels.body:
Imagine your class has a pot of sweets. The teacher lends them out. Each child must give back one extra sweet. That extra sweet is called interest. The teacher can decide how many extra sweets to ask for.
A central bank is like that teacher, but for a whole country. This week, the main banks in America and in Europe are going to decide how big the extra bit should be. Most people think they will keep it the same.
Why might they change it? If everything in the shops costs more, the bank can ask for a bigger extra bit when people borrow. People borrow less, spend less, and prices slow down.
Oil costs more right now. That is why prices are going up.
levels.why: It matters because the price of borrowing affects every family.
